utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Good afternoon, General Galic. Please could you call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before continuing the cross-examination of the witness, I'd like to give a few oral decisions on motions. There's one motion of the 30th of October, Prosecutor's request for protective measures for witnesses. The motion is granted with a few exceptions. In respect of Witnesses H, N, and AE, the Prosecution has mainly given subjective reasons why the witnesses seeks protective measures but no supporting objective circumstances for the request. The Chamber invites the Prosecution to give further information in that respect or to state reasons why it cannot do so. No decision as yet is taken, therefore, on the motion in respect of the Witnesses H, N, and AE. The Chamber has considered in granting the motion in respect to the other witnesses that although a full public character of a trial is of great importance, the measures requested are limited in their effect on the public that wants to follow the proceedings. Apart from not being in a position to know the identity of the witnesses, the measures do not disable the public to follow the proceedings in full. The accused is not limited in the exercise of the rights attributed to him to defend himself. There's another motion of the 30th of October that's concerning the witness which has got a provisional pseudonym AF. The motion is granted, as far as the assignment of pseudonym is concerned, and that any information which identifies him in any public record be expunged from that record. In respect of the request of the witness to testify in closed session, no decision is taken as yet, and the Prosecution is invited to give additional information in respect of the necessity of specifically this measure. And then there's still a motion pending which is a motion of the 29th of October. A written decision on this motion will be given, which will take us some more time, but it's our intention - that's not a guarantee, but it's an intention - to give the decision before the judicial recess starts on the 15th of December, and the Chamber thinks that this will not in any way at this moment obstruct the continuation of the proceedings. These are the decisions on the motions. I further informed the parties that although I do not say anything about other things that have been discussed in closed session yesterday, that we have considered the subjects and we continue considering them. I have to check one of the remarks of one of my colleagues. If you will please give me one second for that. Thank you for your patience. So we have now come at the moment where we can proceed with the cross-examination of witness -- of the witness. Could the usher please bring in the witness, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt you at that point, but it was proposed -- when I broke yesterday, I did not indicate that examination-in-chief was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a mistake. I'm terribly sorry, Mr. Blaxill. We are not yet at the cross-examine. Of course, you can proceed in continuing the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you for that, Mr. President. There is just, however, one thing I would like to raise with the Chamber just prior to resuming the examination of the witness. I believe Your Honours might appreciate at this time, and in particular to the next section of his evidence, the ability to refer to a map of Sarajevo, because you have been given, of course, some visual aid in the course of the opening by my learned friend. But since then, you have not been able to make reference to a map. So it is the Prosecution's intention to offer to the Court and tender to you the visual aids essentially that you had in the course of the opening in terms of a colour map of small scale for personal use, which we distributed to the Court and my learned friends for the Defence, which is essentially a small version of the large map you see on the stand in front of you and also a black and white map of larger scale where the features are more legible and more prominent. So subject to any comment by my learned friends, I do offer you those to be tendered into the Court and for your assistance and reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand the Defence has seen the map and they agree that this is a map that can be used or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I don't believe that the Defence have as such been shown these maps specifically before. They are simply -- they are popular maps, they are public maps. And of course there has been some reference certainly in the course of the opening to the existence of this one which has been seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would allow me to be very practical, I would like to avoid any discussion later as to whether the map is correct or not. We will not take a decision on the admissibility of this map in evidence until the Defence has had an opportunity to look at the map and see whether they could agree with the correctness of this map. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'm not an expert in computers, nor in reading charts or maps. If the Prosecution could help me, what is the scale? I can't see exactly, the scale of the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We will be able to answer that question in just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've seen it, 1 to 12,500. One has to see it from a distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what it says on the top. Any other remarks to be made? Thank you very much. This also might be a moment for me to say a couple of words on documents that have been discussed in this courtroom of which the status is not very clear. We'll sort it out, but this Chamber intends to have some kind of registration of whatever documents that have been shown either during the opening statement or at whatever other moment. But documents that are not intended to be tendered in evidence, but at least later on we know what these documents were we were discussing at that time, although they might have no probative value in whatever way. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder whether that same system could be useful for the purpose of showing an item to a witness at one stage of the proceedings, and then for whatever reason tendering that item as an exhibit at a later point by using the marking system to which you refer, there can then be no doubt that the item which had been shown to the witness is the same as that which is being tendered at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's our intention at least to identify properly whatever document that goes in this courtroom. But I still have to discuss it with the court management. But we'll solve that problem and we'll let you know immediately once we have found a final solution for the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could give a practical example, it might assist you in your deliberations. At some stage in the next few days, the Prosecution proposes to play a clip of video to one or more witnesses and invite them to comment on what appears in the video. But rather than tender the video at this stage, the Prosecution proposes to tender it formally at a later stage, the reason being that as the number of video clips accumulate, they could all be conveniently placed on the one videotape or the one DVD disk at the time of tendering to make it easier for Your Honours and the Defence and the Prosecution to have access to the various video clips. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will respond to that immediately that it should be clear from the beginning of whether it's a video clip or something else, that if it is intended, even if it would be a later stage, to tender it into evidence that it is clear right at the beginning what the status is going to be of that video clip or object whatsoever. We will work that out with the court management and let you know in more detail I hope by tomorrow afternoon. So now, without making mistakes, it's up to the Prosecution to continue the examination-in-chief of the witness. Would Mr. Usher please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac. Can you hear me in a language you understand? I have not yet received an answer. Can you hear me, Mr. Kovac, in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps a unnecessary but, I would like to remind you that you are bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm oblige. Examined by Mr. Blaxill [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac. Are you well rested from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now today, sir, I'm going to be asking you a number of questions on some specific issues, and I will be wanting to focus, if we can, on the period from September 1992 to August of 1994, and not any time periods particularly outside of those dates. As I do so, Mr. Kovac, I will try to keep my questions clear and fairly short, and I would be grateful if you could try and answer as shortly as you can to give the information that you need to give, of course. This will make it, I think, quicker and certainly much easier for the interpreters and for their Honours to get the evidence they need. The first question I would ask you that comes from other matters we had spoken about yesterday was that your Civil Defence people, did they have any form of uniform or working clothes that they wore?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some -- there was some clothing that the Civil Defence people wore, and they were inherited from the times of ex-Yugoslavia, that is to say before the war, and they were worn during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of clothing that was? Perhaps its colour and any insignia that might have been placed upon it.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the blue suits of the Civil Defence with the Civil Defence emblem on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the Civil Defence emblem?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the international insignia of the Civil Defence, with a round logo and a triangle in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the colours of the round logo and triangle?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was yellow with a blue triangle in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac, I'd like to move, if I may, as I said, to the period from September 1992 onwards and ask you specifically about the issue of what protection may have been offered from shelling to the civilians of Sarajevo. Sir, through winter of 1992 and 1993, was there anything in particular Civil Defence was able to do to protect people from the impact of shells or the effects of the impact of shells, I should say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Civil Defence system protected dwellings, apartment buildings especially those that were damaged by the shelling. It was a very hard and difficult winter, and the Civil Defence helped people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything physical they could do to offer actual protection to people from the impact of the shells?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shelters were made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall from 1992 onwards how many shelters you were able to create in the city and whereabouts did you locate those shelters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shelters, in fact, that had been built before the war. They already existed in apartment buildings. And the basements and cellars were of course used as well. They provided shelter. And at least some form of protection. Every apartment building had a basement area, or rather a shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, basically was that the only real way civilians had to protect themselves from shelling, was to go into shelters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've made mention that in the distribution of food and water, you moved the locations where the citizens had to gather to collect it. Did those movements manage to avoid them being shelled?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the aim of it precisely because of the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made a movement from one place to another, did you find that it, then, escaped being shelled or did somehow later that place also receive shelling?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we worked on the basis of the experience we gained, and according to the developments, the circumstances. And as there were a certain number of places that were shelled during the time that humanitarian aid was being distributed, we had to organise ourselves in such a way that we would change the locations where the aid would be distributed, the distribution points, in order to avoid casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you moved from one place to the next, how long would that next location remain safe from shelling, or was it impossible to tell?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a few months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point, let me ask, what sort of shelling, if you're able to say, what sort of shelling was it of those civilian gathering points? I mean, are you able to say whether it was by big guns or by mortars or by some other kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mortars, mortar shells, and they were able to locate their targets even with the protection we set up for the distribution points, because the mortars were able to target indirectly, which means on the basis of maps, the precise location of a target could be determined where people were gathering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that required the use of maps, have you any knowledge as to how the people using those mortars might have accessed those maps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of certain information, some people who worked in the municipality in the land registry department took with them part of the documentation and the maps from Sarajevo. And probably it was those maps that they used to be able to ascertain with great precision where these locations were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as regards my last area on the protection from the shelling of the civilians, were those protections simply using of shelters and moving of distribution points? Were they the only precautions you could take through 1993 and into 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to those precautions, we also made special shelters in settlements and passageways between houses, especially in visible areas, areas that could be seen from the surrounding hills, that is. And by doing so, we tried to provide as much safety and security for the civilians as we could and protect their movements to and from their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may turn to another topic, Mr. Kovac, what about protective measures for the civilians in respect of the sniping that was going on and we have been told about from 1992 to 1994? What measures were you able to take in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of reports coming in to the Civil Defence staff from the various localities in the municipality, and these points were treated as danger zones, and they were usually passageways or the space between two buildings, and that is where a lot of the civilians were killed, passing in between buildings or crossing over, crossing the roads, because they had to move quickly in those zones. And as these were wide open spaces, which meant that they were wide open to continuous sniper fire, when visibility was low, which meant predominantly at night and when it was foggy, we helped set up shelters or protective devices to protect the citizens when they were passing. These protective devices proved to be a little more secure, a little safer, than without them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I stop you there at that point, Mr. Kovac, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I wonder if, Your Honours, we could have the colour map placed on the ELMO for the use of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac, you've made reference to places of -- let's say of particular danger. Could you please indicate to their Your Honours who I trust are seeing this on their screens, could you point to the map and let us know where by September 1992 you may have placed some of these barricades. In other words, which were those vulnerable places?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll focus on the Novi Grad municipality, which is this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, in so doing, Mr. Kovac, I understand that some of the street names will have changed in Sarajevo. There were names at the beginning of the war which were not the same at the end or subsequently. Could you, if there is a place where there has been a name change, could you give us both the old and the new name please, and then perhaps just stick with the new name if you could refer to that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we are speaking about these streets, I should just like to say that they are some of the local communities, and it's easier to pinpoint which places they were. This was particularly vulnerable and open to sniping, that is to say the area of Alipasino Polje. There were apartment houses in Alipasino Polje called the B-phase from the Nedzarici region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kovac, you just said from the Nedzarici region. What do you mean by that reference? What was coming from the Nedzarici region?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several types of -- how shall I put it? Bullets of different calibres, whether they were grenades or anti-aircraft guns, machine-guns, mortar grenades and shells, and ammunition, or rather bullets from sniper weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. There's just one thing I would ask you quickly at this point. You used the expression that translates as a grenade. That can have different meanings to different people. What do you mean by when you use the word the "grenade" what kind of ammunition are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are high-calibre ammunition which is used from -- fired from weapons, from guns, mortars, artillery weapons, multi-barrel rocket launchers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying about that. Yes, please go on Mr. Kovac, about the location you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kovac, would you like to indicate where is the Nedzarici region?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the area here. That's the area, and they shot in the direction of these buildings over here. Furthermore, there was shooting from --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, yes. So from whereabouts did you take protective measures for that area of Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, if you can see this area here, the space between the buildings, that's where we had to put these protective screens up. In Vojnicko Polje, this is now called Vojnicko Polje -- this is now called the district of Sarajevsko Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you make the screens out of at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were for the most part made of spare old car -- spare parts for cars and parts of cars. And also together with some companies that were functions during the war who had -- they had some concrete blocks, so we used spare car parts and concrete blocks. And the civil engineering firm called Vranica, it had these concrete blocks at the Stup locality. The company had some concrete walls, prefab concrete walls, so we used those. And later on, in cooperation with the town authorities and municipal authorities, we asked them for their assistance in erecting these concrete blocks and walls in the vulnerable areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us that when you erected such a barricade, either between buildings or across a street, did that mean there was no further access or was there still a gab left for access to the street or between the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we placed those barricades precisely to enable the people to be able to pass between the buildings and to provide shelter and screen off the area from where the shooting was coming, the bullets that were a threat to the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you approached the task of providing any barricade Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anywhere, what was the first estimation you had to make before you could put the barricade in place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first assessed the danger on the basis of the number of casualties, the people who had been killed at those spots. We saw how many of them there were. And generally, on the frequency of shooting as being a threat to the population moving around those areas. So it was on the basis of those indices that we decided to erect those barricades with the assistance of the people who took part and helped us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now, sir, return to the map, if you would and indicate any other significant places within your own municipality where you erected such barricades and as protection from which directions of fire?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can focus on the Dobrinja settlement now, and Dobrinja is also part of the Novi Grad municipality. It is a characteristic area, a specific one in fact which at the start of the war had a very rough time because for 60 days, the whole district was cut off and exposed to constant shelling and the onslaught and impact of shells, and also other types of attack from other weapons and artillery weapons. The district was attacked from the area of Nedzarici. Here you have it. It's this area over here. That's where the Dobrinja settlement was attacked, and we as the Civil Defence in cooperation with other subjects tried and succeeded in making a channel to link up this part of the municipality with this other region here. And this is approximately where the trench was, trench, corridor. And it enabled people to pass -- to move around from this part of the municipality and go into that other part of the municipality, because this area was open to sniper fire continuously. Also, the district called Svrakino Selo was exposed to sniper fire. Svrakino Selo, as well as the district of Otoka. In addition to other weapons, ammunition fired from sniper rifles targeted these areas here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of barricades and things did you erect in those areas, for protection for civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We put broken-down vehicles there and some other protective material which provided some sort of protection enabling people to be able to pass through the danger zone. We also put up some visual screens in some areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of what you've referred to as visual screens? What were they designed to do?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply people were a bit safer passing through those danger zones because the people who were targeting them couldn't see them, and in that sense, they were protected, so they couldn't be seen when they were moving along those routes and along those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May we just have a moment to confer, Your Honours, because looking at the map we might have something a little clearer to offer on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm obliged to my learned friend for this. As we look at the small map, and especially with the size of the pointer, it is actually, I think, somewhat confusing to delineate quite as clearly as we would like, and it will, I think, lead to a transcript problem that we would not have things quite so specifically cross-referenced to the map. If we may turn and use the black and white enlargement map on the ELMO itself, then I think there will be actual names and things that will be more visible and more legible for Your Honours to see, and I can very quickly recap the various names and locations that I think will help to put this in a bit more clear context. And I'm sorry we perhaps didn't adopt that in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's no opposition from the Defence to use the other map. You have got a copy, or you'll have a copy and inspect it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't any map. We can't see any map. And if we enlarge them, we will have a problem with scale. I think this is an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the scale, I think we can work that out properly. You asked for the scale of this map. It has been reduced already, so I think the original size of the map might be that that's on the board at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can explain the actual manufacture process, that in essence, the small, coloured map is a reduction, the black and white map is an enlargement, and it's all based upon the one map that you see on the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So the scale is the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In fact, I think it's one for one with the large map. It's a straight copy. Yes, the scale is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I apologise, but the map we're using is not very clear, so we would ask you to refer to a clearer, larger map. I wonder if first, sir, you could point to any flag on that map that indicates the area of Novi Grad. Does the name appear on the map? If so, could you point to it.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Novi Grad is -- this is Nedzarici here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold a second. Could you point again to Nedzarici? It's that area there.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, whether there was a building known as the School for the Blind in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then point out, please, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, could we ask the witness to use a pen and to put a letter or something to indicate the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, could you be so kind -- firstly, what colour pen do we have there? I'm thinking in terms of the permanence of this and the visibility of it, for reference. Sometimes markers and things are indistinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think a red one is a better option for future use, Your Honours. Mr. Usher -- oh, you have one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the Nedzarici neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- sorry. I'm not getting the picture on my screen yet. Could you just mark that and perhaps put the letter "A" near the name of "Nedzarici" on the map.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you just briefly indicate now the overall area of Nedzarici with the point of the pen, and draw it. Just draw a line in, what is Nedzarici, as area "A."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you, using the letter "B," pinpoint Alipasino Polje that you referred to. And again, draw a line around that area, and that will be area "B." And could you draw the line around it as to what that area is.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you indicate on there -- just point out the name of Novi Grad, if that appears in the map.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you mark on the map roughly the area where you placed the barricades in Alipasino Polje. Perhaps do a wavy line.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you put on an arrow just to show the direction that you estimated was the place the -- the direction from which the sniping was coming.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where on this map, if you can see it, the school for the blind was, and could you perhaps mark it "SB." Put a cross.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now moving to Dobrinja, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could the map be moved a little to accommodate Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see on this map that there are, twice at least, the word "Novi Grad" appears, and that the witness only pointed to one. This may have its importance. This may be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will address that later on, because that's one of the things that came into my mind as well. Thank you very much. It will be addressed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will obviously ask a question about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just one thing, Mr. Kovac. Before you do anything with Dobrinja, can I just cross-check the initials that were placed on the school for the blind. I mentioned "S" for Sierra, "B" for Bravo. I'm not sure if those were the exact initials written on.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, sir. Now, turning to Dobrinja, can you again indicate where that area lines and draw a line around it and put the letter "C."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again with some wavy lines, can you just indicate some, if not all, of the areas where you erected barricades there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, would you put an arrow on to again indicate the direction of fire, as you would estimate it, that you were providing protection from.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, just above where your hand was a moment ago, I see the letters "Novi Grad" again on the map. What is the significance of the difference between the Novi Grad you already marked and that entrance of Novi Grad you are pointing to now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand quite why we see Novi Grad here. This is the territory of the municipality of Novi Grad. I think this is the Mojmilo hill here. And I think it would be better if we had the word "Mojmilo" written here, rather than Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mojmilo hill within the municipality of Novi Grad? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, well where you say it is Mojmilo hill, would you be so kind as to write in that name for us?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were there any other areas within your municipality that you had responsibility for barricades, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to clear something up. When talking about the competence with respect to barricades, when assessing the need to put up barricades, in addition to the Civil Defence, representatives of the police administrations also participated, that is, of the public security stations in the municipalities who were also responsible for the security of citizens so that a decision to erect a barricade was made at a joint level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Kovac, could I turn your mind to the rest of Sarajevo that was outside your particular district, but looking at the rest of the city, can you point out to us some of the significant spots which were deemed requiring barricades against sniping, particular hazards to the civilians. Can you go through the city and just indicate a few of the spots on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I suggest for ease of reference that each time you mention somewhere, we will number it. So we can go 1, 2, 3, and then you can mention the name and we will be able to cross-refer later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What place is that you have marked as number 1, Mr. Kovac? You'll have to look around to the microphone, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have marked a place next to the school of economics. It's a road leading from Grbavica district to Pofolici. This was a dangerous spot for passer-by, either vehicles or civilians passing through that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which direction did that danger come from for people passing up and down that piece of road? And perhaps put an arrow pointing to the number 1 from whichever direction.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It came from the area of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate any other particular spots in the centre of town that were particularly dangerous?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could list the places. There is the Marijin Dvor point which was under sniper fire from Trebevic, or rather the area of Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, could you mark that number 2, and again put the arrow in for direction.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I find it a bit hard to find my way on this map. But I think when I'm marking this, I am referring to Marijin Dvor

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, if you are unsure, because of the map, please don't mark something if you're not sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, can you tell us any more such places, but only do so if you're sure, with your marking. You needn't...

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can mention Skenderija, also the national theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to point out a specific spot, but can you just generally give an indication which area is Skenderija. Just point to the map if you would.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skenderija is situated about 300 metres from Marijin Dvor towards Bas Carsija along the Miljacka river valley. And that spot, too, was exposed to shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of 1993, were there front lines near that position that you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at Skenderija?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned Grbavica and Skenderija and. Were there front lines in the near vicinity of those places?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark maybe roughly with a pen where you believe those lines were.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And again, you've made reference to an area called Bas Carsija. Whereabouts in the city is Bas Carsija?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bas Carsija is in the old part of the city of Sarajevo. It is well known for its cultural and historical monuments dating back to the times of Turkish rule already, and later from the times of Austro-Hungarian rule times in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's the old part of the city and the city of Sarajevo -- or rather the people of Sarajevo really do have a lot of love for Bas Carsija and admiration. They consider it to be a cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to outline the area of Bas Carsija with your pen, and put the letter -- I think we've reached D now, D for Delta.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac, we've looked very much along so far the South side of the city and along the river. What about north of the area we're looking at now? Were there any particular sniper problems to the north side of the city looking at the top of this map?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems there, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point out any particular areas or locations where you recall there being particular sniper problems which you addressed with barricades?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the old part of the city?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the old part of the city, Bas Carsija, or north of Bas Carsija, yes, and up the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very dangerous, close to the Vijecnica building, the old assembly building. But since the layout of the land there is such, it was possible to successfully target any object in the area of Bas Carsija from the surrounding hills and especially from Trebevic Mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just point out the direction on that map, the direction towards Trebevic Mountain, or indeed identify the mountain if it appears on the map.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you write in the word "Trebevic" on the part of the area that you say is Trebevic Mountain.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay, if we can return, please, could you move the map back down the board again, so down the ELMO, and -- no, stop. Could we see the north side. Could you pull it down so that we see north of the river, please? Mr. Kovac, were there any sniper positions of a particular hazard above the -- where we see the river here to the north on this map? And can you name any such positions? Perhaps I can assist you. Are you familiar with the name Sedrenik as an area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate to us, please, where that may be.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is this area here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that area acquire any reputation in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it known for?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because from that position, there was continuous use of sniper rifles that were shooting on Sedrenik, the broader area of Sedrenik, and the district below it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you perhaps put a ring around the area you've referred to as Sedrinik, and put the letter "S" for Sierra in there, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other such spots like as Spicasta Stijena to the north side of the city?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I couldn't tell you that there were, with any precision. I couldn't tell you the exact spots, but there were some. And surely someone else who has greater expertise about these things will be able to tell you much more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Mr. Kovac. There's just one building. We've heard reference to a place called the Tito barracks. Could you please indicate to the Chamber where the Tito barracks is on that map.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you mark that location that you've circled with "T" for Tango, "B" for Bravo.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Kovac. I won't be referring again to the map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: We had mentioned earlier, Your Honours, the intention perhaps to simply mark for identification certain things. But a lot of information directly relevant to the testimony has now gone into that map, so I wonder if we could in fact tender it in evidence as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited, then, to tender both maps, first a blank map and a second to the map with the initials of the witness on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Indeed. That goes without saying, Your Honour. It's my mistake. I meant both of our maps, obviously, to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're tendering it now? You're not going to use it any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No, I do not propose referring to it in the course of any subsequent witness testimony. I wondered if it might be marked as relevant to the testimony of Mr. Kovac, of course, because at some later date, other witnesses may use other maps, and it may be confusing. So perhaps it at least could be marked not only as a Prosecution exhibit, but as one relating to the evidence of Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Registry will give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have it as the blank map will be 3644 and the map marked by the witness will be 3644.MK.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. Since I hear no objections from the Defence, they will be admitted into evidence, both -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I had expected you to give me the floor to say a few words as to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authenticity of these maps. First, the Defence questions and challenges the authenticity of the maps. During the examination of the witness today and his testimony, we can note that the relevant places have not been indicated, places which are vital in order to be able to assess the testimony of this witness. I am sure you noted that during his testimony, the witness himself said that Mojmilo hill was not inscribed on the map. This Defence counsel knows this area very well, and with a map of this kind, may I say that we're not going to get a true picture of how things stood, which brings into question the witness's very testimony, because the witness said where Novi Grad is is where Mojmilo hill is. That's true, but it hasn't been indicated, nor is there the height, the elevation which is -- it is dominant in relation to Dobrinja as it is to Alipasino Polje and Nedzarici. And this hill is highly relevant because throughout the duration of the conflict in Sarajevo - and this was borne out by the witness's testimony yesterday - this was important because these were the positions of the BH army. So this map does not give us a realistic picture and image of Sarajevo, and it does not contain some very relevant spots. Therefore we object to having these two maps in evidence. This other map, the coloured one, also says "Novi Grad," so the Defence is opposed to having these two maps admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I respond for a moment, Your Honour? Your Honour, may I have a moment to just answer a couple of the points that my learned friend just made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The first thing, Your Honour, is this, that we've just had a look at the black-and-white photocopy map, and it appears to our eyes that there are contour lines on there with figures. And, therefore, I believe if it is an issue at some point, the elevation can be established. However, I think the major point I have is that it is clearly a matter for my learned friend that in the course of cross-examination, she of course can challenge any point as to the map or as to - which I believe to be the thrust of her argument - repercussions made in evidence by the witness as to parts of that map. So I don't believe that that in way taints the map as being tenderable in evidence, as forming part of the evidence of this witness. It can obviously be challenged in cross-examination and by counter-maps that my learned friend may adduce in the future to argue points regarding such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, would you like to respond to these remarks of Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That will lead us to a situation in which this Trial Chamber will have so many maps in front of it that they won't -- we won't be able to find our way. If the Defence team is to give in the same maps, then this will lead to a muddle. I don't know why my colleagues from the Prosecution did not supply you with authentic maps. And I should like to mention in particular that the witness himself says that he finds it hard to find his way and cannot mark the spots where my learned colleague has asked him to -- he says Spicasta -- he keeps referring to a place called Spicasta Stijena, whereas it can't be found on the map. I know what my colleague is thinking of, but you can't find it on the map. So if the Defence team brings its own maps before the Court, this will lead to a mix-up, and there's no need for that because authentic maps do exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision is that the map will be admitted in evidence, but in order to avoid any misunderstanding, this does, of course, does not mean that every single word that's on that map or even the content of that map is as from now not challengeable any more. Of course the Defence will have an opportunity to -- in cross-examination or by producing other maps to make whatever comments or challenge whatever is on this map. But at this moment it is used by the witness, he has marked several spots on the map, so it will be admitted into evidence. I'm quite glad that Defence counsel is worried about the number of maps this Chamber will have to review when deliberating later on. Of course, I would be grateful if both parties could agree upon maps that are reliable as soon as possible so that we limit the number of maps we have to discuss. But the map is -- both maps are now admitted into evidence and get a P number, both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The blank map will be P3644. The map marked by the witness will be P3644.MK.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your indulgence, may I just mention that we agreed yesterday that all the exhibits that the Prosecution intends to tender into evidence during the testimony, that he is duty-bound to supply the Defence with copies. I don't see why my colleagues, if they knew that they would be introducing maps through this witness, why they failed to inform us and hand over those maps to us on time. And as this matter was raised yesterday, my colleagues told me that they would introduce exhibits only through one witness. And at your own proposal, Your Honour, the Prosecution handed over the exhibits for a witness to be heard tomorrow. I am now taken by surprise with these maps because this is the first time that I am seeing them. Perhaps in this heap of material that we did receive those maps exist somewhere. But my colleagues ought to have given me an indication of the fact that they would be using them so that we could prepare for cross-examination on time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber is aware that you have been confronted only recently with this map. And if this would cause a specific problem, the Chamber will -- is willing to hear any objection that comes from being confronted with the map only recently, which is of course something different from the testimony of the witness. It might be that this Chamber, and perhaps the Prosecution, noticed this was a bit unhappy with the situation. A lot of the areas of the city were mentioned recently, and we were not able to follow this on the map. That might explain why a map has come up today. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can confirm that. There was no intention to surprise my learned friend. We just thought in the course of the testimony and with that which was to come, it might have been some help to start acquainting ourselves visually with the city as a layout. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, did the erection of barricades against particularly sniper bullets continue throughout 1993 and into the early part of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, when you had put up or someone or collaborated in putting up these physical protections against snipers, what was the result in terms of human casualties at the location in question?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was greater safety which meant that the number of casualties was much less, and we felt that the erection of these barricades was an effective way of dealing with the situation and protecting the population at certain points in town, which were vulnerable and exposed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Kovac, did at any of these locations, did the amount of sniping actually stop or reduce or stop as a result of barricades?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was lessened. There was less sniping in those localities. But what happened then was that it would be stepped up in other locations so that we were forced to organise the erection of barricades in these other localities as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to other localities, do you mean the just another established sniper area would be more intense or did they in fact -- did you find that new areas became new areas of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they became targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of pattern or particular times when there would be or would not be sniping that you noticed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I hope you don't mind if I interrupt you. You feel that at this moment you are going from localities to timing, which are different areas. And looking at the clock, I would like to have a break at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. I think the order, we changed the order a bit. That means that I will ask the usher to guide the witness out of the courtroom, and then the accused will leave the courtroom, and then finally we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Galic. Mr. Ierace, I see you're standing up instead of Mr. Blaxill. Could you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. I wish to raise an issue in the interests of saving time. Mr. President, you may have noticed that some of the material which has so far been covered by this witness slightly duplicates evidence given by the previous witness. May I make a proposal which may enable us to avoid that in the future. The proposal is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that where a witness called by the Prosecution gives evidence or is in a position to give evidence which has already been covered by a previous witness, that we indicate as much to the Trial Chamber and invite the Defence to state whether there is any issue with the evidence which has so far been given. If there is no issue, then we can avoid duplication and take the witness who is in the box at the time straight to fresh material. If there is an issue, then we can adduce from the witness who is presently giving testimony evidence covering the same area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a proposal. I can imagine that the Defence has to think this over first before responding to it. It might be time-saving, and perhaps you might some have practical problems with it or you might have some theoretical problems with it or whatever kind. If these are just practical problems, I suggest that you exchange views perhaps before tomorrow in the afternoon. If there's any problem left I would like to hear it perhaps at quarter past 2.00 tomorrow. So again, probably think over the suggestion. I can imagine that one of the problems might be to identify exactly those areas where there is no issue, where there is no problem, I can imagine that you would use prior statements of witnesses that are exchanged between the parties, so these practical problems, I would rather whenever possible and see whether you can come to a conclusion. If not, we'll hear that tomorrow in the afternoon and we'll see what would be wise to do. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed we had discussed a moment ago with our colleagues from the Prosecution, we have seen today with this witness that he was not capable to localise certain spots in the city, and this could happen if one were to keep this or that argument could be also against the Prosecution. And there are risks of this being rather tricky, but we are going to discuss and you will have an answer at the requested time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll wait for the answer, then. If there's no other issue to be discussed at this moment, I would like to ask Mr. Usher to bring in the witness, and then Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Obliged, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, we were talking a moment ago about - just before the break, that is - about the timing of sniping during the day. Was there any kind of pattern that developed that you saw during 1993 of when there would be greater or lesser sniping in various parts of the city?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What one could notice is the following --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence objects. The Defence objects to that question by my learned colleague because he's asking the witness whether a pattern existed. The witness has made no mention of any kind of pattern in his testimony so far, nor did he speak about the sniping or the incidents. All he said was that sniping did go on, so I object to the word "pattern" [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll happily rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead, Mr. Blaxill. You want to respond -- I hope you don't mind now and then if we can come to a very quick conclusion without violating the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's a word I've used at this stage that is offensive to my learned friends, I'm happy to rephrase the questions. It may take a couple or three questions rather than a simple one, but I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Even without a decision, go -- rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you indicate to us in what manner the sniping was conducted on the average day?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as shooting of that kind was concerned, it usually occurred during the period when there was no shelling. So when there was a lull in the shelling, the use of weapons such as sniper rifles were used, and automatic rifles and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the weather have any effect on the sniping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they usually took place during the day, although there was shooting at night, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the weather conditions? Did they affect the sniping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if it was more foggy, if the weather was foggy or misty, then the shooting was less intense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the experience that people were only shot on the street where you have said many were, or were there other places that people fell prey to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to shooting in the streets, the snipers also targeted apartments, places where the apartments were facing the line of fire. That means the targets were the windows of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, -- I do apologise. Mr. Kovac, can I ask you, what was the feeling of people who were subjected to the shelling and sniping? What sort of emotions were you aware of in yourself and other people you knew in the city who were living through this shelling and sniping in 1992, 1993, and early 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It left a trace. There was a great deal of fear in the population, and quite certainly, that fear grew as the days went by because there was a great deal of uncertainty. People were insecure. Many people told me that they weren't sure when they would stay at home in their apartments that they'd wake up alive the next day. It was a great psychological burden to bear, with children especially and with the elderly and people especially -- people who were sick and ailing. They displayed this fear in different ways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to us some of the ways that you observed that the people showed their fear?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people quite simply roamed the streets. They would go out into the streets, leave the buildings, regardless of whether it was safe or not to walk around. And there were cases where people quite simply went outside even under fire. They would talk to themselves. That's the way they showed this. Those were -- and you could see that something was wrong with them, that they had become a bit unstable. But generally speaking, the population felt fear, and they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us of any development of these sorts of feelings as time progressed? Was there any difference in the way people felt from the early part, let us say winter, 1992, 1993, to how they felt later in the summer of 1993 or the winter of 1993, 1994? How were their emotions continuing to be affected?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a layman with regard to any kind of medical assessment, I have to say that people were somehow losing touch. They were losing psychological stability. They became phobic. They became claustrophobic. And these effects are felt to this day by people who lived in the city. Most people who are saying they are suffering from claustrophobia fear from leaving closed -- leaving certain spaces or staying in a closed space, and I personally can say that I know how it feels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did people have any particular emotions that related exclusively to the sniping or any aspect of the sniping, as opposed to just the dangers from either shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very hard to draw a distinguishing line because any kind of fire disturbed people and provoked traumas. What I can say is that the children were already talking about snipers, and they knew what snipers were and what shells were. Simply, all this created a war-like atmosphere because the shells were there right next to us. We were living with them, but we never grew accustomed to them. And in addition to physically killing people -- and not only shells but all the other weapons and munitions that we used. So in addition to physical destruction, in my view, drastically more disorders were provoked on -- with respect to the mental state of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your personal emotions, say, towards the sniping, in terms of whom you perceived to be doing it? How did you feel about snipers as people doing what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I had occasion to watch a TV programme. When a child was wounded by a sniper bullet, the father of that child, when he came to the hospital to see his little daughter, he stated publicly, "I would like to see that man who, when selecting his targets and to create some kind of psychological pressure, chose my child, to hit her." So that would be my answer as to how I personally thought about those men who were targeting that kind of weapon on civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you noticed -- in particular you've made some reference to children. Have you noticed any particular behaviour these days as a result of the children's experiences of shelling and sniping during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- firstly then, I will ask you, were your own family and your own children with you in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your family stay with you in Sarajevo during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you noticed any effects on your own children?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of effects have they suffered or have they shown - I'm sorry - have they shown?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that the children were very small when the war started, and there is no doubt that shelling was a new phenomenon in their lives, and they realised that it was something bad. But they were nine months old, little girls. Later, they quickly realised that it was dangerous; and for a time, they never left the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time that -- any time that your children spent or your wife and children spent out of Sarajevo during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what period your family were actually away from the city during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The family was away from the end of May 1992 until the middle or rather the beginning of the second half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from your observation perhaps of your own children and others, can you say anything about their behaviour patterns that you have noticed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the children who stayed in Sarajevo throughout had a more traumatic experience. Today, those children mostly have problems of psychological stability. They are very nervous, they are impatient and are prone to using various medicines. And they have health problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll not be very long, Mr. Kovac. There's a couple of other questions I would like to ask you. One is, have you ever had a personal experience with sniping? Have you ever been close to it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1992, in the winter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that before or after September? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that experience?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bullet whizzed right by my ear at the location of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your feelings when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I felt as if I had been reborn after that, after that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that a little bit more detail for us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to explain a situation when you realised you could have been dead, and it was just a couple of centimetres that separated you from death. The bullet literally flew by my ear, and I heard the sound of it. My feelings after that were -- how shall I put it? I was frightened, I felt upset. The impression was an extremely negative one, and it was a negative experience and very dangerous experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to just move on to some other matters now, three very brief topics, Mr. Kovac. Firstly, did your Civil Defence staff suffer casualties during the work they did between the end of 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many casualties they suffered? Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 200 members of the Civil Defence service that were killed, 200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference earlier, sir, to the emblem worn on the uniform of the Civil Defence as being an international insignia. Was your Civil Defence in some way linked to an international organisation? If so, could you tell us who or what?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cooperated with the humanitarian organisations, with the Red Cross, with the representatives of the UNPROFOR, the United Nations forces. I've already mentioned our cooperation with the French Battalion that was stationed at the Sarajevo airport. We cooperated very well. They came to visit us regularly, and there were no problems at all in that respect. In any event, Civil Defence collaborated with all humanitarian organisations that were present in the Novi Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. But was the Civil Defence, not just in Novi Grad, but in the city or the country, was that linked to other civil defence-type organisations in other countries or places?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that period? There was a certain degree of cooperation, but any significant cooperation or assistance from the international Civil Defence or others was lacking, at least as far as I was aware. But there must have been higher levels of the Civil Defence, such as the republic Civil Defence staff which cooperated with international organisations and institutions and associations of Civil Defence in other countries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I want to ask you just one thing, and that is, at some time, did the barricades that had been erected to protect people, were they taken down at some time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Dayton peace agreement was signed, those barricades were removed because that agreement provided guarantees that there would be no more dangerous attacks on the inhabitants in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see any of those barricades when they were taken down yourself, to have a look at them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a certain number of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the condition in which you found those barricades, let us say, on the one side where the civilians used to move about, and on the other side facing the direction that you thought they needed protection from? Can you tell us what was the condition of the two sides of the barricade when they were taken down?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the side that was exposed to fire was damaged whereas the other side facing the people walking by was clean if -- unless an armoured bullet would pass through the barricade, then the damage could be seen on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell the nature and extent of the damage that you viewed on those barricades, could you tell how that had happened from looking at it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was due to fire being opened from weapons and artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just bear with me if you would, Your Honours, for a moment. That now concludes my examination-in-chief of Mr. Kovac. I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. The Defence has now an opportunity for cross-examination of the witness Kovac. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you started answering questions by my learned friend, and you spoke about snipers. Before I ask you a couple of questions in that area, I would like you to confirm for us whether on the 21st and the 29th of June, 1999, and on the 1st December 2000 and the 3rd of October, 2000, you had interviews with Tribunal investigators. The 21st and the 29th of June, you gave a statement that you signed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's no objection as to the question and I see no reason why you shouldn't answer that question, Mr. Witness -- Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 21st and the 29th of June, 1999 and on 3rd of October, 2000, you had a conversation with the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 1st of December, 2001, you had another conversation with the Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. I didn't make note of those dates, but I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the examination-in-chief yesterday, you told us that after basic training during your military service, you were issued a sniper rifle. You described that rifle. So I have a couple of questions about that. Are you sure that a sniper rifle is the kind of rifle that is issued to a military policeman for performing his duties?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for all policemen. Just a certain number of them. It was not a weapon issued to all policemen but only to some, a number of policemen in the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, a certain number of policemen was issued a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that in a platoon which numbered 30 men, two men were snipers, that is, people who were trained to use a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please interrupt for one moment. Mr. Kovac, in order to have your words properly translated, could you please wait until the transcript stops moving before answering the question, otherwise the interpreters can't do their work properly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood what you said, throughout your military service, you were issued with a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I completed my training, I was issued another weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that training last?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted five months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that training, did you carry the sniper with you all the time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.
